en: A Discourse Supporting the *Guanjing* (Contemplation Sutra), with Preface Composed by Jie Du of Zhu’an The gentleman may be deceived, but he cannot be ensnared;
this was the warning of the ancients. The Great Wisdom Vinaya Master Lingzhi...
The Master often said in his daily life, "In life I shall propagate the Vinaya; in death I shall return to An-yang (Sukhāvatī); thus my duties are complete.
Therefore, while finding leisure to praise and expound his own school, he composed a new commentary on the *Sūtra of the Sixteen Contemplations* to elucidate the teachings of the Pure Land.

Within it, his most refined efforts were directed toward discerning and judging the pure and the mixed, distinguishing principle from phenomena, pointing to the state of mind, and resolving doubts and errors.
This is intended so that those who delight in cultivation may hear it and immediately put it into practice, without having to wait until years of exhaustive study before attaining realization;
it can truly be called a shortcut to rebirth in the Pure Land. All that has been cited herein forms a distinct school of thought, and my primary aim has been conciseness;
thus, I have excised verbose and redundant explanations. Regarding this, the master of the Shanjia tradition, Master Gongyang, remarked that [this work] surpasses...
The study of the scriptures has been fragmented and distorted; when Tiantai’s teachings were attacked through mere words and rejected, it was said that they "aided correct understanding.
As years passed, these teachings nearly reached the point of extinction. It happened that an old friend visited me and I chanced upon this text.

Upon reading it for the first time, it seemed formidable; upon reading it a second time, it became somewhat suspicious; and upon reading it a third time, it was utterly laughable—such a person could indeed be deceived by a gentleman.
Nor should one be deluded; this was the warning of those of old. To support what is correct, one must not merely deceive others but also delude them.
The Tripitaka of sutras and śāstras is common knowledge throughout the world; how could it be that the study of the Vinaya cannot be reconciled with the sutras? What is this but deception?

To extensively cite dharmalakṣaṇa (phenomenal characteristics) and perversely establish difficult arguments—suppressing what is right as wrong and concealing strengths while seeking out weaknesses—is this not delusion?
I humbly reflect that whether one should suppress or exalt [the teachings] in order to assist what is correct and uphold the tradition is not easily determined.

My only concern is that those of superficial learning will accept them at face value and pass them down as mere empty words; with one person singing and a hundred joining in, wavering between two extremes, the fundamental cause for pure karma will from this point forward be obstructed—is this not something to be feared?
I have therefore taken up pen and ink to analyze this matter, and upon completing this composition, I have titled it "Supporting" (Fú).
This new treatise hopes, perhaps, to support the arguments of the new commentary so as not to be deceived by the times.

Though it may be said that one has the intention to resist a carriage with an angry arm, I am truly ashamed to be unaware of my own capacity in trying to block the Yellow River with a handful of earth.

If the principle is correct, what need is there to seek the approval of others? May readers kindly refrain from reproaching this work for its rash simplicity. Written on a spring day in the year Wuxu.
Regarding the preface to the *Dongxi Huayushu Zu'an Xu*, Fu Zheng said:
"Because the practice of not receiving the temporal teachings according to the new commentaries has become an extreme弊 (corruption), I shall first explain it."
The Treatise says: From the time Buddhism first came from the West during the Eastern Han dynasty until the Qi and Liang periods, its origins and currents gradually expanded.
Those who propagated and expounded it were more than one or two in number, each having their own lineage of teachers and successively following the teachings of their predecessors.

Thus, our Way has continued in an unbroken succession; those among them who cultivated realization and attained awakening are fully recorded in the official histories—yet at that time, [the specific doctrines discussed here] had not yet been heard of.
How flourishing is the teaching of the Tiantai school regarding the temporal periods of the Dharma!

Even if one were to claim that all those of the "three schools of the south" and "seven schools of the north" are entirely refuted by it, what of the fact that after the passing of Tiantai, masters such as Xianshou and Cien arose like pillars, each establishing their own distinct lineages?

How could they not have known of the Tiantai doctrine of the temporal periods of the Dharma? Yet, we have never heard of them following it. Furthermore, consider the holy masters of India, such as Vasubandhu; [the same applies].

Generally speaking, those who have produced commentaries have each established their own distinct systems. For instance, Nāgārjuna’s exposition of the *Prajñāpāramitā* divides it into two paths, while Aśvaghoṣa’s commentary on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* (the *Yijiao jing*) organizes it into seven sections.
One should not, therefore, dismiss these as erroneous simply by applying the criteria of Tiantai’s "Teachings According to Time" (*shijiao*).

This is especially true in the case of Qingliang [Zongmi], who personally studied the Tiantai teachings under Jingxi [Zhanran] yet nonetheless established his own distinct lineage and opened up competing portals.
The windows are newly opened and unobstructed; yet, since this is not the Tiantai school, how can one demand that it follow the Tiantai system of *shijiao* (temporal teachings)?
Does this mean that the *shijiao* established by Tiantai is unreasonable? Generally speaking, it depends on the individual’s choice; how can one suppress them and force them to accept it?
One should know that the Buddha-dharma is like a great capital city: from east, west, south, or north, people may come and go as they please. Indeed.
If one wishes to ensure that all people in the world follow a single path, as seen in the governance of a state, how could this be achieved?
If my new commentary were to strictly follow the Tiantai system of temporal teachings (*shijiao*), what need would there be for a separate exposition?

It is simply because from antiquity until now, the distinction between the pure and mixed teachings of the two lands has not been clarified, resulting in a total confusion; it is only through my new commentary that [this distinction is made].

Because he was able to understand this and assist in rectifying it, he was rejected for not accepting the teachings at that time; indeed, to use one's own views to obstruct others without first knowing whether such an act is appropriate is improper.
The *Xinshu* (New Commentary) states:
"The various masters each venerated their own sectarian traditions, so that later students did not know where to turn; I have now selected the most excellent [elements from them]..."

Having extensively eliminated the superfluous and the cumbersome, I have selected the best from among the commentaries and sub-commentaries composed by Master Yuan of the Sui dynasty, Tiantai Zhiyi, and Shan Dao, as all of them possess profound meanings;
therefore, I have followed their excellence in my current exposition.

Fuzheng said: "Since the gradual eastward transmission of our teaching, the study of Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras has lacked clarity regarding the temporal context of the teachings and the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox;
thus, it has become the companion of the Pāśupata school.
The new commentaries are superficial and destructive to our teaching, yet they claim to expound the sūtras through subtle words and profound meanings, labeling them 'verbose. For instance:"

Regarding the word "Buddha" in the title, there are the Dharma-body, Reward-body, and Response-body Buddhas, as well as the Buddha of Birth and the Buddha of Dharma, each with its own degrees of excellence or inferiority;

to which of these Buddhas does the present sutra belong? Furthermore, regarding the word "contemplation" (guan) in the title, there are the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional, the contemplation of entering the conventional from emptiness, the contemplation of the Middle Way and the Supreme Truth, and even the contemplations of the True Suchness of the *Zhan-cha* and the Consciousness-Only (*Vijñaptimātra*) teachings. As for the title itself— [the text continues].
Regarding the observation of which category these characters belong to, the *Lun* (Treatise) states:
"Tiantai judged and explained the various sutras of a lifetime through the Five Periods and Eight Teachings;

the 'Three of the South' and 'Seven of the North' were as if unheard of and ignored—how could anyone dare to propose a comparison between them? Furthermore, the *Zhuan* (Biography) composed by Nanshan praised Ling..."
Zhiyi likewise took up his pen to offer praise; yet, as for what is called "eliminating the superfluous" in the present commentary, is this intended merely for the *Tiantai* period teachings?
Rather, it refers to the style of composition itself—striving solely for brevity and propriety without indulging in prolixity.
As the preface to the *Xuanxue* says, "I have omitted the weeds and gathered the refined blossoms," and the preface to the *Shujing* says, "I have cut away the profuse."
To haphazardly clip and prune away flowery rhetoric—especially when considering that the Preface to the *Jingxi Lueshu* states: "The brush was held by an attendant;

there were indeed many redundancies, and those who saw them might fall into the fault of admiring such prolixity. Since the text often carries meaning through its phrasing, if it is verbose, one must prune the words.
Jingxi was a disciple of Tiantai; that he permitted even his master’s writings to be edited and pruned truly reflects the universal principle governing literary composition.
This is the constant rule throughout antiquity and the present: even when a new commentary critiques a predecessor, there are naturally masters within that lineage such as Huiyuan and Shandao;

why then should one be partial only to Tiantai? Furthermore, if one does not clarify the temporal teachings (shijiao), one becomes a companion to the Pāśupata heretics, as in the examples previously cited of Nāgārjuna, Aśvaghoṣa, and the various masters of Western India, including Maitreya.
Is it truly the case that all those who follow the precedent of the "Gracious Sage" (Enken) have fallen into the ranks of the heterodox?

Furthermore, those who raise objections regarding the two characters "Buddha-Contemplation" (Fukan) do so solely because they fail to distinguish between the differences in the teaching traditions of the two lands;
consequently, they conflate the modes of practice and realization of this land into a single whole, which results in every movement being obstructed by doubt. Now, even if one were to say...

The five periods, eight teachings, three bodies, four lands, the single mind and three contemplations, and even the immeasurable dharma-gates, are all established as the fundamental tenets of Tiantai;
what connection do they have with the new commentaries?
The *New Commentary* states: "In the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, it is exclusively Mahāyāna;
among those born there, there are none who do not resolve upon the unsurpassed bodhicitta, and all attain the stage of non-retrogression.

From this we know that the two lands differ in their establishment of the teachings—whether pure or mixed—and thus there is no need for laborious selection or judgment regarding the various sutras on the Pure Land. Tiantai says: "This is the Mahāyāna Vaipulya [Vaipulya-vaipulya]."

"The teaching subsumes the two *piṭakas* and clarifies their meaning; the Bodhisattva gathers those of gradual and sudden enlightenment and leads them into this, which is the Sudden Teaching" (and so forth).
The *Fuzheng* [commentary] states: "The beginning of the new commentary claims that the Pure Land is purely Mahāyāna and thus need not be distinguished or judged.
Although the Pure Land is indeed purely Mahāyāna, the intent of the scriptural passages that distinguish it lies in indicating the ultimate destination for practitioners in this land."
The *Xinshu* (New Commentary) merely follows the perspective of those already born in that land [Sukhāvatī] and does not judge the scriptures intended for those to be born in this land.
Since it states that [the Pure Land teachings] are "exclusively Mahāyāna," this already excludes the partial and the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). Why then does it say, "one need not trouble oneself"?
Since these words are appropriate for exclusion and judgment, they possess the name but lack the actual meaning; how can one neglect the Tiantai division of the teachings?
Next, he cites Tiantai’s interpretation of the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka* regarding how to comprehend the meaning of "sudden" (*dun*), noting that there are many paths to this (and so forth).

Furthermore, he observes that the meaning of "bodhisattva" itself has many varieties (and so forth), providing an exhaustive citation from the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (and so forth), concluding with the question:
"With what kind of mind, employing what kind of contemplation, does one destroy what kind of delusions?"
"Into what stage does one enter? (and so forth). The Commentary states:
"Is it not the case that the New Commentary’s claim that the Pure Land is exclusively Mahāyāna constitutes a definitive judgment (*viniścaya*) of the scriptural texts?

Is this definitive judgment of the scriptures not intended as the ultimate destination for practitioners of this land? It is precisely because those who have already been born in that land [are addressed]."
Since these people are exclusively of the Mahāyāna, they cause the scriptures for rebirth in this land not to be combined with or limited to the vehicles of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha;

once the teaching has arrived, how could it be divided into two? Yet, [some] claim that one should only rely on those already born [in the Pure Land], rather than the scriptures for those to be reborn there.
The New Commentary clearly judges that the Pure Land is exclusively Mahāyāna, further citing Tiantai’s *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) regarding the Mahāyāna Vaipulya.

If one relies on that which is called "not laboring to issue a definitive judgment regarding the arising of life," and furthermore knows that the phrase "the newly expounded Pure One Great Vehicle" already constitutes a definitive judgment, one fears encountering the objections of others;
thus, one shifts the argument, saying: "This very phrase is itself the definitive judgment.

As for what [Nā] says, "no need to labor," it simply means that this is not like the lands of this world, where one must labor to distinguish between the Great and Small Vehicles, the Partial and the Perfect, one by one.
If one carefully examines how the teachings on the Pure Land encompass all things under a single principle—since they are none other than Mahāyāna—it need not trouble you.
However, if, like the *Fuzheng* (Correcting the Auxiliary), you insist on making distinctions and judgments, then consider those scriptures that exclusively discuss the Pure Land:

there are seven such sutras. I wonder which among them are Mahāyāna and which are Hīnayāna? If they are all indeed Mahāyāna, then it is identical to the new commentaries; there is no need for further labor.

To distinguish and judge [the teachings] by claiming that if both the partial and the small [vehicles] are included, this conversely reveals that the Pure Land is not yet the Perfect and Sudden—such a relentless pursuit collapses of its own accord.
Furthermore, to say, "Next, citing Tiantai’s *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-saṃgraha*, how is this to be understood?

and even to say, "The meaning of 'sudden' has many paths, and there are many types of bodhisattvas," is precisely what is called deception. One should know that this refers to the *New Commentary* (Xinshu).
What has been established here is simply the direct application of the correct principle through no other path;

for it is based on the fact that Vaidehī, without passing through the minor fruits, immediately realized the non-arising of dharmas, and is thus termed one of "sudden capacity. Since she belongs to the Sudden Teaching, how can its principles, practices, and fruits be compared with the stages and positions of the Small Vehicle as found in the *Abhidharmakośa* and *Vibhāṣā*?
A square peg does not fit a round hole; I do not know how such a comparison could possibly be made.
It is indeed so. For the most part, Fuzheng relied upon his own powerful rhetoric as if no one else existed; he refused to acknowledge other schools, honoring only his own learning.
Without distinguishing between the new commentaries (*shu*) that circulated in the world, he sought to prevent them from being extinguished.

Thus, he laid out the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics) and piled up scriptural teachings, arbitrarily citing heterodox views and fabricating empty arguments to ensure that the lineage of the new commentaries would have no place to stand.
If one were to place their hands and feet there and retreat in fear, not daring to speak or discuss it, then this would mean that the new commentary naturally sinks into oblivion.
If one exerts oneself in such a manner, is it to deceive others, or is it to deceive Heaven? The new commentary states:

"A thousand years from now, there will surely be those who can appreciate its true sound; how could one allow private sentiments to obscure it? It further asks: "With what mind and with what contemplation shall one approach it?"

Regarding the question of which delusions are destroyed and what stage is entered: it is precisely because one fails to distinguish between the differences in entering the Path in the two lands that such a statement is made.
One should know that those who are reborn in the Pure Land are for the most part the multitudes of ordinary beings still bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*).
As the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata now [speaks] for the sake of all sentient beings of future ages who are being harmed by the thieves of affliction."

This refers to the teaching on pure karma. Furthermore, it is said: "If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all sentient beings are oppressed by the five sufferings of the turbid, evil, and unwholesome [age], how shall they behold Amitābha Buddha and the Land of Ultimate Bliss? Tiantai says:
"Those born in that land are not necessarily all those who have attained the Way; therefore, the Sūtra speaks of those who have committed grave offenses at the moment of their death."
At that time, by repenting of one's sins and reciting the Buddha’s name, karmic obstacles are immediately transformed, and one attains rebirth [in the Pure Land].

If only the sages were born there, how could ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) aspire to be born in that land? Thus we know that even while possessing defiled afflictions, one may still attain rebirth there. (Text) Siming also said:

"Without departing from the present thought, one aspires to reach that region, so that even as an inferior ordinary person, one may immediately ascend to the stage of non-retrogression. He further said: "Right here..."
Even those of ordinary capacity can rely on superior conditions to achieve rebirth and never again fall back (text).
According to this sutra and its commentary, it is clear that once one has reached that land, one then cultivates the supreme path and only then discusses the refutation and manifestation [of truth].
If one has already destroyed delusions and entered the stages while in this land, why would one need to seek rebirth in a pure land? *Fuzheng* merely wishes to refute and reject the new commentaries.
Not knowing how to turn back toward the public truth, they instead contravene the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
The *New Commentary* states: "To realize that Pure Land is precisely one's own mind and not another dharma;
to reach that Amitābha is precisely one's own nature and not another thing. It continues: "The pure and defiled bodies and lands are all sentient beings."
One’s own mind is such that, because the substance of the mind (*citta-tattva*) is empty and pervasive, its coming and going are unimpeded;
and because the substance of the mind is all-encompassing, its grasping and rejecting are without hindrance.

*Fuzheng* says: "The calculations of the new commentary do not go beyond the substance of the mind being empty and pervasive, and the nature of the mind being all-encompassing within that pervasiveness."

That there is coming and going within what is all-pervasive is the ultimate discourse on the Pure Land; when one’s insight reaches this point, how does it differ from the calculations of externalists?

Even the heterodox outsiders claim that the lands of the world are contained within [the self], and they say, "I pervade the ten directions, unmoving and serene, while all sentient beings are born and die within my own heart. Such is the talk of the new commentaries.
Furthermore, by what distance do these non-Buddhists reckon [the gap]? Moreover, the "illusory-transforming mind" discussed within the Hīnayāna is but a partial aspect of the Dharma-realm;
why then is it singled out for exclusion? Nevertheless, this sutra is the definitive meaning of the Mahāyāna, encompassing the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha and the rebirth of ordinary beings.
For those of shallow understanding whose samādhi is not yet perfected, if they were to give rise to such a view, what purpose would it serve?
The mind distinguishes between the heterodox and the orthodox.

The Commentary states: "The New Commentary discusses this exhaustively; it is evident that it reaches this very point. To assist what is correct is to bring about the beauty of human perfection; it is not merely to foster human evil.

Yet, some cite similar-sounding words to muddle these most appropriate meanings. For instance: [The text continues with a critique of a specific interpretation regarding the nature of the Buddha-body.]
The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) arise entirely from the deluded mind of birth-and-death; their false calculations do not transcend the notions of causality or spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
As for the Hīnayāna, it is a mind of birth and extinction that analyzes phenomena to realize a partial emptiness.

Since they have never even heard the names of the bodies and lands of other Buddhas, how could they believe in the teaching of the nature of the mind-only? The principle [of this teaching] is far removed from them.
How can Mount Tai and the tip of an autumn hair be compared as being of the same order? Knowing this to be impossible, he again shifts his argument, saying:
"Nevertheless, regarding this sutra’s status as the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the Mahāyāna," etc. One must know that this statement is even more inconsistent and remote from the truth.
Why? Because the practice in this land proceeds entirely through one's own power, relying on the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) to investigate and exhaust delusion.
Because of consciousness, there arises the false interpretation that past karma is initiated;

if one cultivates pure karma, it is entirely dependent on the power of others, as Amitābha Buddha’s vow and light constantly come to gather and sustain them, ensuring that demonic activities will certainly not occur.
Furthermore, this confusion and intermingling results from failing to distinguish the differences between the teachings of the two lands.
The New Commentary states: "The Tiantai Commentary says that this sutra takes mental visualization as its primary tenet; this refers specifically to the subject who visualizes.
Master Yuan, Shandao, and others all take the samādhi of Buddha-visualization as the primary tenet;
this establishes it by encompassing both the subject and the object."
Fuzheng said: "The new commentary claims that Tiantai read the text incompletely by focusing solely on the 'one who contemplates.

However, since the subsequent text states that 'taking the wondrous contemplation of cultivating the mind as the primary principle,' how could this refer to focusing solely on the 'one who contemplates'?

For the meaning of 'cultivating the mind' through wondrous contemplation is based on the principle that 'this very mind creates the Buddha' and that the Buddha manifests within the mind; therefore, it is called 'cultivating the mind.'"

Since the words of "wondrous contemplation" (*miao guan*) are none other than *samādhi*, one knows that the wondrous contemplation for cultivating the mind and the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* (contemplation of the Buddha) cannot be distinguished by means of the categories of subject and object, or the single and the multiple.
The Treatise says: "Whenever one intends to determine right from wrong or evaluate gain and loss, one must rely upon the manifest text; only then, beneath the text..."

In seeking the meaning, there is not a single instance of error in this new commentary; thus, the reasons for distinguishing and judging the scriptural tenets of the two schools are based on the explicit text itself.

As for the *Fuzheng* (Correcting the Auxiliary), it instead cites the subsequent passage and provides a circuitous interpretation based on its meaning, wishing to include both the subjective capacity (*neng*) and the objective object (*suo*).

Now, I say that the phrase "wondrous contemplation of cultivating the mind" in the subsequent passage is no different from the previous discussion of "mind-contemplation" (*xin-guan*). As I perceive it, since [the Master] of Tiantai has already...

Regarding the discussion of the inherent nature (xingju): the present single thought-moment is fully endowed with the three thousandfold world of phenomena and reality, including the physical bodies and lands, as well as the causes and fruits of sentient beings and Buddhas.
Though small as a hair-tip, it is vast as empty space; raising one part, the whole is encompassed. There is nothing that is not the nature of mind.
Apart from the subjective observer, there is no separate objective realm. If this is so, even if Tiantai had focused solely on the subjective observer, it would have been excellent in itself. Why?

One must certainly rely upon [the teachings], for this requires both the subject and the object; moreover, since this new commentary takes the contemplation of the Buddha as its primary tenet, it strictly follows the *Ten Doubts* (Shiyi lun). That text states: "All who seek rebirth should give rise to a longing mind and form mental images, taking as their object the physical marks and radiant light of Amitābha Buddha, and further contemplating the adornments of the seven treasures of that land," as detailed in the *Sixteen Contemplations Sūtra* (*Śrī-akṣobhya-vyūha-sūtra*). The New Commentary states that it takes the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha as its primary tenet, citing sutras and śāstras to establish proof, and further clarifying the relationship between principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*), stating:
"Principle is a provisional name for the void and quiescent; phenomena are specific designations for conditioned activities. Those of sharp faculties understand this.
In principle, all is but mind; those of dull faculties who have not yet reached ultimate realization rely exclusively on the practice of phenomena.
To assist this, the *Xinshu* (New Commentary) states that its primary tenet is the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*. This scripture clarifies that there are three grades of Buddhas, namely:

those eight chi tall, those one zhang six chi tall, and those with eighty thousand marks and signs. Among these three grades, it is for the purpose of visualization [that this teaching is established].

Regarding the names of the samādhis in this section, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are one hundred and eight in total, beginning with the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, followed by the *Mahā-vipula-samādhi*, the *Siṃhavikrīḍita-samādhi*, the *Abhibhū-samādhi*, and so on, up to the nine kinds of samādhis in the *Bhūmisaṃgraha*.
The new commentary mentions only the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*; I do not yet know by which samādhi one should contemplate which Buddha.

Regarding how the *Ten Doubts on the Treatise* (Shen-so-chun-shih-i-lun) is to be received and applied, the sequence for clarifying the two contemplations—of phenomena (*shi*) and principle (*li*)—is as follows.

This is based on a passage from the *Sūtra of Examining the Grounds of Contemplation* (*Chen-cha-ching*), which states: "First, those of sharp faculties should practice the contemplation of the true suchness (*tathatā-satyālambana-vipaśyanā*);

those of dull faculties should first practice the contemplation of mind-only consciousness (*citta-mātra-vijñapti-vipaśyanā*). Is it not the case that true suchness is the principle, and mind-consciousness is the phenomenon?
The *Xinshu* (New Commentary) states that those of sharp faculties who practice through principle-observation (*lǐguān*) realize that all is but mind (*weixin*).

The Treatise says: Regarding the Buddha-contemplation samādhi (*guanfo sanmei*) established in the *Xinshu*, whether it be eight feet, sixteen feet, or eighty thousand feet, one should observe according to the depth or shallowness of the practitioner’s intellectual power (*zhili*).
If one is suited to observing eight feet or sixteen feet, then one should observe eight feet or sixteen feet; if one is suited to observing [the vast form], then one should observe [it].
If there are eighty thousand [forms], one should contemplate those eighty thousand; for this reason, the sūtras specifically establish three grades [of practice].

How could one definitively determine which grade to contemplate in all cases? Furthermore, while the name "samādhi" is common to many, when it is used here as "contemplating the Buddha" (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*), it is already distinguished from other samādhis.
Why then do you ask, "By means of which samādhi does one contemplate which Buddha-body? According to the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*...

The Doubts and Discussions clarify that the essential meaning is by no means obscure; yet, you have withheld the full text of the new commentary and instead ask how it is to be applied. Where is your public-mindedness?
Regarding the two types of contemplation—phenomenal and principle—as cited from the *Sūtra on the Divination of the Auspicious and Inauspicious*, the difficulty lies here:

if one claims that "mind-only" belongs solely to the level of principle (*li*), I fear this describes the name while missing the essential intent. Let me explain this for you: one must understand that what is shown in the *Sūtra on the Divination of the Auspicious and Inauspicious* pertains to both the phenomenal (*shi*) and...
If the principle is based on the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) to speak of directly penetrating the *dharmadhātu*, it is termed "arising from principle" (*lir qi*);

if it involves mental investigation through deliberation, it is termed "arising from phenomena" (*shi qi*). Although these two differ, they are both nothing other than the cultivation of contemplation; the distinction between the two is merely made in terms of the initial arousal of the mind.
The *Xin shu* (New Commentary), however, is not like this; it is a general discussion of all phenomena and principles, rather than being restricted solely to [the initial arousal of the mind].

Consider, for instance, the sixteen contemplative objects (*ṣoḍaśa-vipaśyanā-viṣaya*): there is nothing among them that is not a manifestation of the environment and inhabitants (*niśraya-saṃbhoga*) of that land.

They do not differ in their pervasiveness across phenomena (*vastu*) and principle (*tattva*); rather, they appear differently according to the practitioner’s contemplation. Those of sharp faculties realize that the objects are merely mind (*citta-mātra*), and thus everything is principle;

those of dull faculties mistake the mind for objects, and thus everything is phenomenon. This distinction between phenomena and principle is made based on whether the mind and its objects are deluded or awakened. If...

When this current commentary is compared with that *Zancha jing* (Sūtra on Divination and Observation), it becomes clear that the present *Vijñaptimātratā* (Consciousness-Only) system can naturally encompass both contemplations of that sūtra.
In the "Chapter on Repentance" of the *Nanshan Shishi Yaolu*, it is discussed how the cultivation of *Vijñaptimātratā* is also divided into two distinct types based on where one directs one's mind.

This current commentary follows [the precedent] by extensively citing the textual passages from the *Zancha jing* within the *Zizhi ji* to demonstrate the specific characteristics of its cultivation; it is not that [the author] was unaware of this, but rather [he acts] accordingly.

How could literary usage and function possibly be treated as mere clichés? Furthermore, since the term "mind-consciousness" (citta-vijñāna) applies to both phenomena and principle, and is extensively discussed in the sūtras and śāstras, why do you see in the *Zancha jing* a sudden division into two types of contemplation and judge them as belonging exclusively to the phenomenal level?
If one understands the arguments established in the *Xin shu* regarding the refutation of the *Fujian lun*, one will see that they have no connection whatsoever.
The New Commentary states: "By this we know that contemplating the Buddha’s immeasurable merit is the vanguard for repelling evil and the initial gateway for entering the Way.
*Fuzheng* says: "The New Commentary itself declares that the method for attaining Buddhahood in the Perfect and Sudden Supreme Vehicle is 'the mind is the Buddha.'"
According to this present sutra, as soon as Vaidehī heard it once, she shattered ignorance and attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
If one takes a definitive teaching from among the definitive teachings as merely a preliminary array or an initial gate, what then could serve as the ultimate dharma?
The Commentary states: The New Commentary specifically highlights that the merit of the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha is transcendent and unsurpassed, uniquely ranked as the foremost;
therefore, it is called the "Vanguard" and the "Initial Gate. This itself is the ultimate Dharma; it does not mean that there is some other separate ultimate Dharma.
I request that you examine the New Commentary, which cites various sūtras in succession to provide evidence for contemplating the Buddha, and only then will you see [the truth].

My ultimate aim was not to exhaustively investigate the meaning of the text, and thus these words were formed in a casual manner. This was because this particular phrasing happens to coincide with that in the *Tiantai Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts).

Therein, the functions of the three trainings are discussed in succession: since the precepts merely stop evil and prevent transgression, they are called "the initial chapter for mobilizing goodness" and "the vanguard army for repelling evil.

It is only through concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) that one can truly destroy delusions and manifest the principle; thus, they are considered the ultimate. I have merely surmised this.
The Auxiliary Corrected Edition mistakenly interprets that passage and thus makes this statement:
"The New Commentary says: 'I have examined the scriptural text and find it merely presents the objects of contemplation without distinguishing between phenomena and principle;
could this not be because the practitioners who contemplate them differ in their faculties—some being sharp and others dull—and thus enter [the path] differently'?"
Fuzheng said: "This is a contradiction of one's own words. Below, he himself explains the scripture: "This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha.
He says that "mind" refers to the practitioner’s mind that contemplates the Buddha. Through contemplating the marks of the Buddha, those marks appear within the mind, and so on, until he says:
"I fear it might be thought that the accomplishment of Buddhahood through cultivation is obtained from without; it is simply because this mind, in its very essence, is [the Buddha]."
The Buddha therefore said, "This mind is Buddha. Regarding such an interpretation, is it based on principle (*li*) or on phenomena (*shi*)? Is it neither principle nor phenomenon?
If one says it refers to phenomena, then as for principle, the preceding text itself states that "phenomena and principle are not divided"; what, then, would be included in the contemplation?

Furthermore, since the text itself explains, "The essence itself is Buddha," is this not a contemplation of principle? The sections from "Contemplating the Sun" (*ri guan*) onwards involve striking at the mind.

Is the object not itself the contemplation of phenomena? Furthermore, since Vaidehī requested instruction on my "contemplative thought" (*cintā*) and "right reception" (*samādhi*), both of which belong to the subject who contemplates, how could it be that you speak of only a single object without anything further to which one might turn?

The Commentary states: It is truly unacceptable for those who assist the orthodox yet are confused and agitated to disregard the contextual flow and provenance of the text, picking out a single word or half-phrase to raise objections.
This is because various masters of past and present have offered biased interpretations of the sixteen contemplations;

some say that the sixteen sublime objects are nothing other than contemplations of principle (*li-guan*), while others say that according to the beginning and end of the sutra, they are all [contemplations of phenomena].

Regarding the "Phenomenal Aspect" (*śarīra-lakṣaṇa*), one version states that the fifteen [sections] before and after constitute this matter as the ninth. Because the Buddha contemplates these phenomena as principle (*tattva*), he generally rebukes [the previous view] by saying:

"The first explanation omits the middle and subsequent sections. Next, in interpreting those [sections], it suppresses the superior faculties [of those who would cling to them]. Furthermore, the subsequent division into two parts is even less a comprehensive treatise; thus, there is the underlying intent for the present text.
This means that the objects of contemplation (*ālambana*) discussed from beginning to end throughout the entire sutra cannot be judged in a partial or biased manner.

This depends solely on the practitioner’s degree of acuity or dullness in their cultivation. For those of sharp faculties, every object is principle; for those of dull faculties, every object is phenomenon.

This is precisely what the *Xinshu* (New Commentary) establishes by defining the objects and instituting the contemplations, thereby dividing them into subject and object so that practitioners may enter accordingly without bias toward either phenomenon or principle.
It thus aids the correct path, yet [the opponent] instead uses the contemplating subject to challenge the contemplated object, posing a counter-question.

Whether this pertains to principle (li), to phenomena (shi), or to that which is neither phenomenon nor principle, though I have taken up my pen to forcefully attempt a detailed analysis, I cannot help but burst into laughter.
The new commentary states: "It is known that both mundane and supramundane dharmas are none other than the wondrous principle. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says:
"Contemplate all dharmas as empty, their true reality (yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa)," and again: "All dharmas are utterly non-existent," as well as the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
If it is said that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows;
as the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* states, "All dharmas are themselves the Buddha-dharma"; as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states, "All dharmas are the aspect of bodhi";

and as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states, "All dharmas are without arising and without cessation," and further states, "One thoroughly knows that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all dharmas is non-existent."
If one were to discuss the sublime principle apart from all phenomena, one would fall into partiality and heterodoxy.
*Fuzheng* says: "These seven passages are cited to prove that the sublime principle is discussed without being separate from all phenomena;

furthermore, the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra*, the opening passage of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*—the meaning of these three texts allows for [the principle] not being separate from all phenomena."
Regarding the remaining four passages, such as the citation from the *Lotus Sūtra* stating that "one contemplates all phenomena as empty":

since this is cited as scriptural evidence, how can one say they are empty while not being separate from all phenomena? Furthermore, regarding the subsequent citation stating that "all phenomena are non-existent," this is because they are detached from all forms of existence;
thus it says they are "all non-existent. How could this mean they are not separate from all phenomena?
Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka* states that one must thoroughly understand that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is non-existent and that even their existence is absent;
only then does one see the essence of Śākyamuni. The text of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* likewise teaches that the essential nature is fundamentally empty and entirely unobtainable.
These four passages all declare that all phenomena are empty and non-existent; this alone is the sublime.
Lina asked: "Is it not the case that one discusses the subtle principle without departing from all phenomena?

The Treatise says: The New Commentary, fearing that practitioners of the末代 (final age) might abandon the world of dependently originated phenomena to seek the subtle principle elsewhere—thereby falling into the view of annihilationism—has specifically cited seven passages to inspire faith;
indeed, it is nowhere other than by manifesting the principle through phenomena itself.
The realization that delusion is entirely true means that all Mahāyāna principles converge upon a single principle;

yet, while the *Fuzheng* (Supplement to the Correct) permits only three texts, it claims that the remaining four texts [imply] that all phenomena are empty and utterly non-existent. This meaning should be understood as "not departing" from the *Li* (Separation).
Now, I ask: how can one who studies the Tiantai path under Master Fuzheng hold such a view? Take, for example, the four...
The emptiness of all phenomena discussed in the scriptures is not the same as the great void, which is devoid of even a single thing.

This is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), wherein phenomena are manifest yet are truly empty; they are non-empty yet wondrously non-existent. How can one establish a fixed doctrine of emptiness and existence?
If it were as the *Fuzheng lun* (Treatise on Correcting Deviations) suggests, it would resemble the biased emptiness of the Hīnayāna or the nihilism of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
I do not know what the intention behind this [view] may be.
The *New Commentary* states: "The contemplative methods elucidated throughout the teachings of the one lifetime of the Buddha can be summarized into five general categories:

first, the general contemplation of all phenomena, as the Sūtra says, 'contemplate all phenomena as empty'; second, the specific contemplation of one's own mind, as in the *Cessation and Contemplation for Returning to the Source*."
First, observing only form, as the sutras state: "Contemplate the true mark of the body; contemplate the Buddha likewise.
Second, observing both form and mind together, as the sutras state: "Clearly perceive that the five aggregates are all empty.
Third, observing sublime objects, such as contemplating Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in various sutras.
Fuzheng said: "One version states: 'Regarding the general contemplation of all dharmas, we now ask: at the time of employing contemplation, what dharma is being contemplated?
Is it one dharma that is contemplated, or are all dharmas contemplated?
If it is one dharma that is contemplated, does it belong to form (rūpa) or to mind (citta)? Mind is the same as the second case; as for form, [it is the same as the first case]..."
The third meaning is the same: if one contemplates all dharmas, since all dharmas are immeasurable and in a state of total confusion, how should the practitioner apply their mind?
It continues, even stating: "By inferring from this, there is absolutely no point of reference."
The Commentary states: The method of contemplation elucidated in the new sub-commentary comprehensively encompasses the modes of practice taught throughout the Mahāyāna of all periods;

it summarizes them within five categories so that nothing is left out. Its intention is to distinguish and clarify that this present sutra belongs to the fifth category, thereby preventing confusion or overlap.
This merely indicates their names and characteristics for now; it does not yet definitively discuss the cultivation of contemplation or how practitioners should proceed.

Whether one practices cultivation, consults a virtuous teacher, or investigates the sacred teachings, one will naturally attain understanding; why then do you find it difficult to practice the method of meditative observation now?

As for your objection regarding the inclusion of terminology and its results, the opposite is actually seen: your critique merely serves to corroborate the point that the state of mind and its objects are in total confusion, leaving one with no clear direction—this fault does not lie with the new commentary.

The New Commentary states: Question: May these sixteen contemplations now be termed "contemplating the mind"? Answer: If one has realized that objects are nothing but mind, then which of Amitābha’s bodies or lands would not be mind?

However, I fear that if one instead seeks the original *skandhas* and restricts the recognition to a specific point of spiritual consciousness, then all such practices belong to other sutras and are not the primary contemplation of this [text].

Fuzheng said: "As for what you call 'seeking back to the origin,' 'localizing within the yin realm,' and 'recognizing the point of spirit' as belonging to other scriptures—how could those other scriptures ever be so localized?
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says, 'Let the mind roam through the Dharma-realm like empty space,' and it also says, 'There is nothing in all the worlds that does not arise from the mind.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says, 'The mind pervades the ten directions,' and it also says, 'The wondrously luminous, original mind.'"
How could such scriptural passages as "the essence of mind is all-pervasive and perfectly round, encompassing the ten directions" be considered merely a localized point regarding the numinous spirit?

This sutra also states, "This mind creates the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. This is no different from other sutras' discourse on the pervasive nature of the mind's substance, being non-dual and without distinction.
Why then would you regard the *Oguan jing* as superior while disparaging the Great Canon?

The Commentary states: Since the new sub-commentary establishes the visualization of the Buddha as its primary tenet, it specifically clarifies the questions and answers that harmonize this with the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*), such that neither is obstructed.
However, the present contemplation of the mind differs from that of other sutras;

those other sutras describe contemplations for entering the Path within this land, which do not grasp external objects and further exclude other dharmas such as the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), focusing instead solely on one's own single thought-moment of delusion.
Is the mind not precisely the localized recognition of the numinous point? This is what the new commentary indicates as the place where the practitioner directs the mind and sets out;

it is the most vital gateway for entering the principle through contemplation. Yet, while examining the text closely, one finds that instead of providing detailed analysis, the author merely cites various passages to issue a refutation.
One should know that if the cited passages were not discussing the primordial state of equality, [the refutation would be misplaced].

The essence of the impartial mind (*samacitta*) is precisely the manifestation of the principle of the perfection of contemplation; how could it have any relation to the doctrines established in the *Xin shu* (New Commentary)?
Furthermore, the citation from the root scripture stating "the mind makes the mind" is consistent with various other scriptures in one sense, yet not so in another.
Let scholars investigate this for themselves to discern its merits and defects.
The New Commentary states: "First is the Buddha of the samādhi of one’s own mind; second is the Buddha who has realized the fruit from causes in the Western Quarter.

While various sutras teach that contemplating the mind means contemplating the Buddha seen within one's own mind, this present sutra specifically teaches the contemplation of the Buddha who has realized the fruit from causes in the Western Quarter," and so forth.
Fuzheng said: "This sutra itself states that 'this mind makes the Buddha' and 'this mind is the Buddha.
Why then do you close your eyes to interpret its meaning, claiming that the visualization in this sutra is a result induced by causes rather than conforming to the Buddha’s own words?"
The Commentary states: Regarding the two Buddhas cited by the ancient masters in the New Commentary, that passage from the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) continues by saying:

"Now, possessing both meanings together as a single object, these two Buddhas must be identical from the perspective of principle (*li*) and distinct from the perspective of phenomena (*shi*). In reality, they are not two;
however, because the New Commentary follows the tenet of the Sūtra and requires one to contemplate those Buddhas, it cites the two Buddhas of the ancient masters."

The distinctions are thus clearly delineated, so that practitioners may find a point of reliance for their minds. When the state of samādhi is perfected, one realizes that the Buddha is not outside the mind;
because one sees the Buddha through the mind itself, seeing the Buddha at such a time is called seeing one's own mind.
To see one's own mind is to see the Buddha-mind. Only at that moment can it be said that "this mind creates the Buddha" and "this mind is the Buddha."

The New Commentary states: "To establish [the doctrine] with not even a hair’s breadth of error—this is what is meant by 'not adhering to the Buddha's words while closing one's eyes to explain the meaning.
To attribute such a crime to others is itself a sin.

The New Commentary further states: "First is the Dharma-nature Land (dharmatā-kṣetra); second is the Responsive Transformation Land (nirmāṇa-kṣetra). Within the Responsive Transformation Land, three divisions are made."
This refers to the Land of True Reward, the Land of Expedient Means, and the Land of Common Residence;
it is also said that "emptiness arising within great awakening" refers to the Dharma-nature Land, while "leakage-filled lands of subtle dust" refers to the Responsive Transformation Land.
Fuzheng said: This single passage contains roughly two errors. First, it contradicts the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Zhilun) which he himself cited;

for since that treatise states that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are born within the land of skillful means (*upāya-kṣetra*) and receive the dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*), how could a dharma-nature body reside within a minute particle of dust? Second, it alters the traditional explanation regarding the heavens.

Since the *Taisū* (Platform Commentary) already clearly explains the four lands (*catur-bhūmi*) without differing from what is taught in the *Shinsū* (New Commentary), why does it omit the old names and fail to explicitly employ their meanings?
It merely establishes them by way of the two lands of Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) and Responsive Transformation (*nirmāṇa*), and only subsequently opens out the four lands.
Furthermore, since the *Shinsū* employs the four bodies (*catur-kāya*) from the *Kaishū* (Precept Commentary), why does it not explicitly employ the four lands as well?
The treatise states:

Throughout the commentaries and sub-commentaries of past and present, there are numerous instances where citations and interpretations are omitted or selected; whenever these accord with the text, they are cited.
This is the art of adapting to the occasion—what could be right or wrong about it? How can one restrict oneself to a single corner [of interpretation] as if it were a new commentary?

The reason for employing the Tiantai doctrine of the four bodies (*catuḥkāya*) is that the passage on the four bodies in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) merges seamlessly with the sūtra; thus, it may be utilized.

The *Shu* (Commentary) quotes the sūtra as follows: "The Dharma-realm body (*dharmadhātu-kāya*) of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas refers to the Dharma-body and the Reward-body (*dharmakāya* and *sambhogakāya*). The sixty million billion bodies refer to the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
It may manifest a great body of one zhang and six chi, or eight chi, or even [the forms of] ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, and so forth."

Regarding the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), its name and meaning have been adjusted accordingly. The subsequent clarification of the lands is based solely on the fact that there is no textual evidence in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts).
Therefore, [Fujiao] states: "Since the *Jieshu* clearly elucidates the four lands, why does the new commentary omit the old names?
To this, I now ask: where in the *Jieshu* is there a clear explanation of the four lands? Please examine this.

To fail to understand this and instead further deceive others is truly lamentable. This is because the various sūtras clarify the lands so extensively that it is difficult to present them all in detail;

therefore, their essentials have been cited and the categories of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) condensed so that the meaning may be easily perceived. Thus, they are explained by means of the two lands of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) and the responsive-transformation (*nirmāṇa*).
With the exception of the land of Dharma-nature, all other realms of dust and lands are subsumed within the responsive-transformation land. However, this explanation is not without its basis.
The scriptural authority cited here is the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, which states: "Within the Great Awakening, emptiness arises like a single bubble emerging from the ocean;

the myriad lands of outflows are all produced based upon emptiness. The commentary explains this itself, stating: "Great Awakening" refers to the Dharma-nature Land (*dharmatā-kṣetra*), while the "myriad lands of dust-like atoms" refers to the lands of response and transformation (*nirmāṇa-kāya*).
This illustrates the skillful mastery of appearing and disappearing, or accepting and rejecting, according to the timing of circumstances. The meaning is found therein.

Although this new commentary establishes its system for a single period, it likewise follows established models. For instance, in Tiantai’s *Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, there are two sections:
a general explanation of Buddha-lands and a specific explanation of Buddha-lands. Within the general explanation, it states: "Lands have both phenomena and principle;

phenomena refer to the realm of the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), while principle refers to the sphere illumined by ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*). This is taught merely to respond to the capacities of sentient beings.

Because there is both the Real (the *dharmatā*) and the Responsive (the *nirmāṇa*), the principle and phenomena are clarified; continuing thus until it says: "Because they manifest traces, there are responsive forms and responsive lands;
because they reveal the fundamental [nature], there is the Dharma-body and the true land. Next, the four lands within the central [classification] are explained individually. The text states:

"The various manifestations through which the Buddhas benefit sentient beings are immeasurable and boundless; now, for brevity, they are summarized as four: first, the defiled-pure land; second, the land of residual conditioning (*sopadhiśeṣa*)."
The three are the lands of retribution, and the fourth is the land of eternal quiescent light.

One should know that the initial section of the New Commentary, which distinguishes between the Dharma-nature body and the response-transformation bodies, is generally consistent with the meaning of Tiantai’s "comprehensive explanation. Furthermore, the subsequent subdivision of the various lands within the response-transformation bodies is consistent with the meaning of Tiantai’s "detailed explanation.
Since Tiantai already possesses such systematic standards, why do you fail to reflect carefully before rashly refuting them?

As for the refutation of the claim that this contradicts the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is not a contradiction with the new commentary; rather, it is a shortcoming in the *Fuzheng* (Supplement to the Correct).
One must understand that although Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas may dwell outside the realms, their dharmatā-body and land have not yet shattered ignorance, nor is their dharmatā fully perfected;
they all belong to the category of "transformative birth" (*parināmika-jāti*) within the "remainder of skillful means. This is when viewed from the perspective of the ultimate.
How could the land of the principle of *dharmatā* not be composed of motes of dust? "Motes of dust" is merely a metaphor for its vast abundance.

Fuzheng failed to discern this; seeing the mention of "motes of dust," he immediately equated it with the defiled realms of the mundane world and exclaimed, "How could the *dharmatā*-body dwell in a land of motes of dust? How so reckless!"
The New Commentary states that Vaidehī requested, "Teach me how to contemplate; teach me how to enter right concentration.

The Old Commentaries respond by assigning the three blessings to contemplation and the sixteen visualizations to right concentration. However, Shandao says, "Various masters combine the three blessings with contemplation and the sixteen visualizations with right concentration;
I say this is not so. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states, "It speaks of contemplating right..."
"Receiving" (*śīla*) is another name for "samādhi"; thus one knows that "contemplating right reception" (*samyak-samādhi*) is simply a request for instruction.
Master Fu Zheng said: "Since Vaidehī requested 'contemplating right reception,' the Buddha answered with the 'Contemplation of the Auspicious' (*bhadrā-vipaśyanā*).

This is because the essential points correspond; the text neither expands nor contracts. Even if there is a claim regarding alternative names in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, that belongs to its own specific translation."

What purpose does human ingenuity serve in relation to this sūtra? In the exegesis of sūtras, it is indeed common to cite other sections; yet if the meaning of the sūtra is already manifest, what need is there for such cross-referencing?
Let me illustrate this with a single example: the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* exists in two different translations, one from the Liang dynasty and one from the Tang.

That translated by Paramārtha is known as the "Liang Version of the Saṃgraha," and therein he establishes a ninth consciousness called the "eternally true and pure consciousness" (*tathatā-viśuddha-vijñāna*).
The Master’s translation of the *Triṃśikā* does not establish a ninth consciousness; rather, it states that the ninth is merely another name for the eighth.
If this were the case, consider those who propagated the Liang dynasty’s *Triṃśikā* in later generations:

when they saw the Tang dynasty’s *Triṃśikā-bhāṣya*, did they claim that the Liang version only established eight consciousnesses? For this reason, although the new commentaries on this treatise rely upon Shandao...

Regarding what has been said—whether the fruit of the "unknown" (ajñāta) and the "skillful guide" (sukhāvatī) is so or not—our own school’s exegesis of the sūtras already employs the phrase "Excellent!
Excellent! (*sādhu sādhu*), using identical words to express a "double praise" of the provisional and the ultimate;
how much more so for the clear correspondence between *samādhi* and *saṃjñā*, which cannot possibly be interpreted otherwise?

The Commentary states: Regarding the phrase "contemplative meditative attainment" (*cintā-samādhi*) as explained in the New Commentary, even if one had not seen Shan Dao’s *Xuanyi*, it should simply be interpreted according to the explanation of "requesting contemplation.

Why is this? Generally, in discussing the cultivation of contemplation, one must first give rise to mental deliberation to discern and determine that the object and the contemplation are not erroneous before entering right contemplation.
However, as long as the mind and its objects have not yet been forgotten, it still belongs to the stage prior to [right] contemplation, namely, "contemplative" (*cintā*) [attainment].
This is the skillful means (*upāya*). When the mind and its object merge into one, the contemplation is perfected and the principle becomes manifest; this is termed "right reception" (*samādhi*).

Those who offer this explanation base it on the commentary to the sutra text, which quotes the passage on the "earth-contemplation": "One who forms such an image is said to have a coarse vision of the land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss"—this refers to the stage of reflection (*cintā*).
If one attains *samādhi*, one sees the land of that country with perfect clarity and distinctness, such that it cannot be fully described.

Since "explaining" (*shuo*) refers precisely to "correct reception" (*zhengshou*), it is said: "Even if one does not perceive the profound meaning (*xuanyi*), one should simply proceed by requesting the 'Explanation' (*shi*).
How much more so since the *Xuanyi* clearly contains this statement, which accords with the text like two halves of a tally; thus, it may be cited to establish the present argument.

It is only because the two phrases of Vaidehī’s request do not appear explicitly in the text that Shan-dao feared people might hold divergent interpretations, and therefore [he specifically addressed this].

Citing alternative names from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* to explain this, one should reflect upon the term "contemplation" (*cintā*). In many texts, this refers specifically to "right contemplation" (*samyak-dhyāna*);
for instance, the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna* states: "With right mindfulness, contemplate the single reality realm," and further says:

"Contemplate the Mahāyāna mind without ceasing. The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) also states: "Contemplation is right contemplation. Furthermore, as seen in various texts, the eightfold right path is subsumed within the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*).
The *Daoshi* (Daozhi) commentary attributes "contemplation" (*sīwéi*) to wisdom (*huì*), while the new commentary takes it as "vision" (*jiàn*).
However, after Queen Vaidehī’s request, the sutra text is interrupted for nearly half a page before it states, "If one wishes to be born in that land, one should cultivate the three types of merit.

This does not explicitly take up the previous question to provide a dual response to her request; therefore, it is appropriate to explain this as "auxiliary to the Path" (*zhùdào*). This interpretation is based on the Tang dynasty [commentary].

From the time of the Venerable Shandao until the present, several hundred years have passed, yet the profound meaning (*xuan-yi*) he established continues to be practiced in the world. Prior to this, we had never heard of such refutations;
why then do you now harbor resentment toward a commentary that merely adopts and utilizes the interpretations of others?

As for the example you cite—comparing the distinct names for consciousness established by the two *She lun* treatises of the Liang and Tang dynasties to the distinct names for the various samādhis—is it not the case that you are now borrowing their very example to turn it back upon yourself as a counter-argument? What is the point of your concealment?

Regarding this, although the Liang dynasty’s *She dasheng lun shu* (Commentary on the Mahāyānasamgraha) views the Tang dynasty’s *She dasheng lun shu* as asserting that the "nine consciousnesses" are merely alternative names for the eight consciousnesses, it never relied upon their functional application to establish nine consciousnesses as an auxiliary to the orthodox system.
Why, then, must the new commentary force one to follow the Tiantai school by answering the contemplation [of the mind] with the three types of merit?
Furthermore, although it cites alternative names as examples, those examples are inappropriate. Why is this? Because what has been called "ancient" since time immemorial...
The schools of the Southern and Northern Dynasties each held their own positions, with the Liang and Tang schools establishing their views based on correct conditions.

Whether they asserted eight or nine consciousnesses, or whether they took them as real or false, they refuted and established one another like water and fire. Therefore, although the Tang school’s inclusion of nine [consciousnesses] claims it is merely a different name for the eight, it is appropriate that the Liang school’s inclusion does not rely upon it.
Now, in order to clarify the scriptural text, Shan Dao has come forward; his *Huayan* [commentary] perfectly accords with this.
Since this is consistent with the [preceding] context, it is employed accordingly; how could it be the same as the dispute over the two types of inclusion (*saṃgraha*)?
Furthermore, regarding the citation of the two lines beginning with "Excellent" (*sādhu*) as an example, this too does not constitute a comprehensive argument;

it merely concerns the provisional and ultimate teachings of the two cycles—the Dharma and the Parable—within the *Lotus Sūtra* as understood by the four great śrāvakas, which led the Wise One (Mañjuśrī) to offer his double praise. This is not the case for other sūtras.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "To speak it twice is the height of excellence. The Chan Master of Xiachuan, commenting on the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, says:
"To say 'Excellent' twice is the ultimate of goodness. Furthermore, how is this so?
The New Commentary states: "Regarding the practice of the Pure Land, no māras can cause affliction; this fully enumerates the various masters' teachings on the absence of māras.
While entering the Way in this land involves encountering māras, none of the sūtras concerning the Pure Land mention them at all.
Thus, it is clear that this dharma is free from māras."
Fuzheng said: "Is it not true that among the various sutras concerning the Pure Land, those which do not mention Māra are few? The *Ghoṣadatta-sūtra* states:
'The father of Amitābha Buddha, the Arhat Samyaksaṃbuddha, was named King Candra-vimala, a Wheel-Turning Sage King;
at that time, the Māra-rāja was named Ajita. This is the word of the Buddha. That there is a Māra in the Pure Land is refuted by the new commentary."
How vast is the difference between saying there is no Māra and the new commentary! The treatise states:
Whenever one wishes to establish discourse and transmit instruction to broaden the gateway of the Teaching, one must first observe the general course and not be constrained by minor details.
Furthermore, if that Pure Land of Peaceful Nurturing were subject to Māra, it would be no different from this world of five turbidities.
How are they different? The reason why the various scriptures and treatises do not mention Māra is precisely because he assists the Righteous One as his basis.

The *Drum-Sound King Sūtra* states that there are Māras in the Pure Land; this is likely based on the fact that one has not heard the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which also contains the teaching that Amitābha possesses lands that are not strictly pure.
Consequently, such false claims have arisen. One should know that those sūtras are in fact manifesting the [reality of] Amitābha.
Regarding the comparison of their merits and defects, let us briefly cite one matter from the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* to contrast them.
That sūtra describes the land as being ten thousand *yojanas* in extent, whereas this sūtra describes the body as being sixty million billion *nayuta* Ganges-sand *yojanas* in height.
How could that inferior and lowly land possibly contain such a vast and tall body?

The Heavenly Master [Zhiyi] specifically verified that this scripture clearly manifests impurities; therefore, both Gushan and Hexiuan, relying on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, cite that scripture as saying:
"Amitābha Buddha was of the Brahmin caste, his mother’s name was Viśeṣamati, and he also had a rebellious disciple named Devadatta.
Since there were women and a rebellious person, how could Amitābha not be [subject to such conditions]?
(Question: Does this mean that a defiled land is being manifested? (Text: Master Ciyun also once analyzed this, saying: "In the *Ghoṣadatta-sūtra*, it mentions the Buddha’s mother, Viśeṣacāritrā.
Does this imply that there are women in the Pure Land as well? (Answer: It is likely that "the Buddha’s mother" refers to the time of his descent [into the womb].
After he attained perfect enlightenment, the land necessarily became pure, and thus there would certainly be no women. His mother may have subsequently been transformed [into a male].
If a man dies in such a manner, or if a dragon girl passes away, it will be like the mother of Siddhārtha. (Text) Ciyun has provisionally analyzed this based on one specific case regarding women;
since he cites the *Drum-ghoṣa-rāja Sūtra*, other cases may be understood by analogy. Now, one should apply the same principle:

the mention of the Māra King likely refers to the time of his descent from heaven [into the womb], for after attaining perfect enlightenment, his land would be purified accordingly, and there would certainly be no Māra.

Furthermore, in the *Ten Doubts* (*Shiyi lun*) by Tiantai, it is stated in the fourth section on the five types of non-retrogression: "Externally there are no ghosts, spirits, demons, or heterodoxies;
internally there are no three poisons or afflictions" (text). Jingxi, in his *Miaole*, says: "Even in the Buddha-lands there are differences in grade;
since there are no women, there are certainly no evil realms. Or, even if there are women at times, there are still no evil realms. As it is said: [End of quote]
Although the land of Akṣobhya Buddha has women, there are no female afflictions; in the land of Amitāyus, both are absent.

(Text) Regarding the "two kinds," this refers to women and the evil realms (*durgati*). Since Māra is subsumed within the evil realms, and it is stated that both are absent, how could Māra possibly exist there?
The orthodox teachings of the Buddhas and Patriarchs are as clear as the midday sun; they all state that in the Pure Land, [neither women nor Māra] exist.
The Māra has never consulted [the original texts] and instead rebukes the new commentary for its lack of learning; those who observe this may well laugh.
The new commentary states: "Some say that if the mind is pure, it is itself the *svabhāva*; why then seek it in the West?"
Regarding the claim that there is no such principle as being born in a pure land of another direction:

this refers to the *dharmatā-rūpa-kṣetra* (the realm of the nature of phenomena) within the teachings, rather than the pure land elucidated in the present sutra. For an ordinary person bound by all fetters who has not yet attained the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), even if they were to achieve sudden enlightenment regarding their own mind, who could constantly maintain purity?
Although the Dharma is supremely sublime, it does not encompass all capacities of sentient beings; however—
[The opponent asks: "If there are merely empty words, how can one enter [the truth] through them?

Fuzheng replied: "The *Lotus Sūtra* is sublime and wondrous; its ultimate and heroic discourse is nothing other than the Wondrous Vehicle (*samyak-yāna*), for it is entirely the self-nature (*svabhāva*).
How could it be mere empty words that do not lead to entry? For what reason would such a sublime and wondrous teaching fail to encompass all capacities of sentient beings? Alas!"
To slander and profane the venerable scriptures by claiming that the principle of *dharmatā* and the land of the teachings within this doctrine are not the Western Pure Land—

why is it that the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta* states that those who hear this chapter will, at the end of their lives, go directly to the world of peace and bliss where Amitābha Buddha resides? Furthermore,
if hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* leads one to birth in Amitābha’s land, is this not the very body of the sublime Mahāyāna scripture?
Since there is nothing among the teachings and practices of the Buddha that is not subsumed [within it], how can one say that the Western [Pure Land] is not the Dharma-nature land?

It is even said that the *Tiantai* school’s practice of the wondrous contemplation of the mind takes the realization of the four pure lands as its primary principle; thus, the wondrous exhaustion of the Mahāyāna, which encompasses all things, is none other than the Western [Land]. (And so forth.)

The Commentary states: Generally, when discussing the body and land (*kāya-bhūmi*), there are inherent distinctions between horizontal and vertical, and between identity and difference; it is not appropriate to conflate these into one.

This is a case of "differentiation without differentiation" and "non-differentiation within differentiation. To investigate thoroughly, they are ultimately nothing other than the single *dharmatā-ratna-bhūmi* (the Jewel Land of the Nature of Reality).
Yet, this *dharmatā-ratna-bhūmi*—known as Vairocana—is omnipresent throughout all phenomena, such that there is nothing that is not the Buddha.
Every school of Mahāyāna asserts that all phenomena are inherently complete within the Dharma-nature; how could this principle belong to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* alone?
This truth is so luminous and sublime that it transcends the mental capacity of ordinary beings. As the Sūtra says, "Only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land"—this is precisely for this reason.
Yet, many people in the world rely upon the sacred teachings to indulge in grandiloquent and superficial discourse.
One might then claim that because the mind is pure, the land is pure, and thus there is no need to initiate cultivation. For this reason, the *Xinshu* (New Commentary) criticizes such a view, asking:
"There are merely empty words; by what means can one enter [the path]? How can you say this does not slander the sutra?

Regarding the passage from the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-parivarta* cited as evidence for rebirth through hearing the sutra, if you refer to it as the "land of the principle of dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*), why is this so excessively abrupt? If one speaks of it in terms of principle (*li*), there is nothing that would be incorrect.

If one speaks in terms of specific phenomena (*dharma*), it may be feared that this is not necessarily so. Why? For instance, the Dharma-nature principle-realm (*dharmatā-tattva-bhūmi*) is precisely the Constant Quiescent Light (*nitya-śānti-prabhā*).
Within this Constant Quiescent Light, how could there be such names as "Sukhāvatī World" or the "title of Amitābha Buddha"?

One should know that while there is no division, it is nevertheless divided; thus, it is appropriate to refer to the *sahab-hāva* Pure Land and the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of Amitābha. Furthermore, it is said: "All..."

That "nothing is not the Western Land" is likely because one has failed to investigate the teachings of the Pure Land and, deviating from the standard path, has consequently produced this superficial and misleading statement.
If everything were indeed the Western Land, why would Vaidehī have had to humbly petition Śākyamuni repeatedly for the sake of the final age?
And why would Śākyamuni have manifested his light in that land to allow Vaidehī to choose her destination at will?
One should know that the new commentary (*xin shu*) distinguishes these matters with great clarity and integrity; those who bear the Dharma in mind should examine it in detail.
The new commentary cites Chen Xu Ling, who said: "I wish to return immediately to the human realm and take rebirth in a place that is neither high nor low.

This was a Confucian of the secular stream and not one held accountable for his words; yet among the masters of the Chan and Dharma-exposition schools, most hold this same view, all claiming that [one will be reborn] hereafter.
The World-Honored One did not fail to address the man who had left home to study the Way, saying to him by way of trial:
"Now that you have already attained birth as a man and have left home, you ought to seek further liberation; why then do you again seek to be born as a man and wish to leave home once more?
Is there truly no superior progress?"

Fuzheng said: "The new commentary speaks without reckoning the resulting distress and calamity. Even if there were a deluded person who formed such a view and set it down on paper and brush, one would simply dismiss their school;
how much more so for those who have plumbed the depths of Chan and the subtle teachings—men of virtue whose words must be authoritative.
How can they be conflated with such [views] to expose their lack of evidence? Should people hear or see this, slander and confusion will proliferate, yet they remain unaware."
Those scholars of that school who have traditionally censured such perverse and contrary views ought to correct them.

The treatise states: "In my new commentary, I observe that among the followers of both Confucianism and Buddhism, though they claim to study the Buddha-dharma, they lack insights that transcend their respective schools and surpass conventional patterns;
they are mostly mired in ordinary sentiments. Therefore, when I offer bitter admonitions and guidance to lead them, they instead respond with partisan attacks and denunciations, saying:"
